This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}$ be the Fibonacci sequence. Let $n_1<n_2<\cdots $ be an infinite sequence with $n_{k+1}/n_k \geq c>1$. Must\[\sum_k\frac{1}{F_{n_k}}\]be irrational?
#267: [ErGr80,p.65]
irrationality
It may be sufficient to have $n_k/k\to \infty$. Good [Go74] and Bicknell and Hoggatt [BiHo76] have shown that $\sum \frac{1}{F_{2^n}}$ is irrational - in fact,\[\sum \frac{1}{F_{2^n}}=\frac{7-\sqrt{5}}{2}.\]Badea [Ba87] proved that $\sum \frac{1}{F_{2^n+1}}$ is irrational. 
The sum $\sum \frac{1}{F_n}$ itself was proved to be irrational by André-Jeannin [An89].
The main problem has been proved for $c\geq 2$ by Badea [Ba93]. It remains open for $1<c<2$.
Additional thanks to: Kevin Barreto

 Note that this special case is significantly easier to establish irrationality for than general cases, because of the well known divisibility relation that $F_n | F_m$ when $n|m$, so each denominator here is a multiple of the previous. So this series is similar to the series $e = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n!}$ for the purposes of establishing irrationality.

A full proof 
claimed by Colin Snyder (using GPT 5.6 (custom harness)).
 Summary:
 We claim the answer is yes for the full range: for every index sequence with $n_{k+1}/n_k\ge c$ for some real $c>1$, the sum $\sum_k 1/F_{n_k}$ is irrational. Proved in Lean 4 / Mathlib (theorem erdos_problem_267), standard axioms only, no sorry. For $c\ge 2$ this was classical (Badea, 1993); the open case was $1<c<2$.
Idea: suppose the total is rational. The identity $1/F_n=\sqrt5\sum_j(-1)^{nj}\varphi^{-(2j+1)n}$ rewrites the series as an integer coefficient word over $\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]$, and rationality pins its residuals to a fixed lattice. Comparing two suitable windows of the word then produces a nonzero element of $\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]$ with norm strictly between $0$ and $1$, which cannot exist. Deep dyadic structure in the indices is deleted exactly first, and a CRT density argument locates the required windows, with an explicit cutoff.
 Notes:
 The $c\ge 2$ range is prior art (Badea's criterion); the contribution is the full range $c>1$.
